items.title: Emmanuel Sayles Interview, 1959-01-17
items.q: well I was going to school I was going to 35 school and this is in 1924 and I think it was the month of April because I was in 9A and when they told me about this job I was all enthused about it... we finally we went on the job we left New Orleans with George Morris as the manager Mike as the trumpe

ctx.x: yeah so uh like I said we were rehearsing with these Mac Thomas Mac George Morris and Edmund Hall you see and uh we used to play out this place the colored place out in Polyland this is during Prohibition now and I remember we had numbers like uh uh what were you that those days you played you had to play your tiger or that but you didn't play as fast and you had to play Sister Kate and there was those easy numbers yeah easy numbers uh the bucket got a hole in it that was a good jump number we had back in those…

items.title: Emmanuel Sayles Interview, 1979-12-05
items.q: And so we got this job, a fellow named Joe Wynn came to... So this man came to the, and he decided to take us. His name was Joe Wynn.

ctx.x: When did you start playing music professionally for, you know, your first few jobs?

Well I wasn't calling myself a professional before, before 24. I was in ninth grade, 35, right there, F1-0. And these two guys was taking lessons. This man and these guys were married men and everything. They left in the days first. The Trammer played George Morris, and Trump was played Thomas Mack. And the saxophone player, Edmund Washington. I just buried them this year, first part of this year. And they used to get a little job, they used to hire me. They had family and everything. I mean, they were work guys,…
Yeah. So you decided pretty much in Pensacola that, or?

items.title: Emmanuel Sayles Interview, 1961-01-29
items.q: So, uh, they had some trouble about their money with Prince Morris, and this fellow, Joe Wynn, he, uh, he took Al Morgan and, and, uh, Edmund Hall out of that band. Oh, yeah. See, and put them with us.

ctx.x: And we used to rehearse around there and we used to go to the trombone house and rehearse. I was on 8 and Liberty and I had a cousin, Ray Fielder. And he was playing drum, but every Sunday, remember, we used to rehearse on them. And some fella came in town by the name of Joe Wynn, looking for a band, and they got in the word of it. And so they made a deal with him. And the only thing about the deal was this fella, Joe Wynn, played drum.
